t: LeetCode 2062 - Count Vowel Substrings of a String: Vowel Runs and the atMost Trick
o: **Understanding the problem.** A vowel substring consists only of the letters a, e, i, o, u and must contain all five; we count how many substrings of word qualify. In "aeiouu" both "aeiou" and "aeiouu" (starting at index 0) qualify, so the answer is 2. In "unicornarihan" no stretch of vowels manages to include all five letters, giving 0. In "cuaieuouac" the vowel run "uaieuoua" hosts seven qualifying windows. The bound of 100 characters makes checking all starts feasible, yet the run structure - consonants terminate everything - also yields a linear two-pointer solution built on the classic atMost(k) subtraction trick.
k: A vowel substring can never cross a consonant, so candidates live entirely inside maximal vowel-only runs.
Containing all five vowels is equivalent to having exactly 5 distinct characters.
Exactly-5 = atMost(5) minus atMost(4): the subtraction isolates windows reaching full vowel diversity.
A bitmask over the five vowels turns membership checks into O(1) operations.

a.n: Approach 1: Bitmask Scan From Every Start
a.i: Start at every vowel and extend through the current vowel run, folding each character into a 5-bit mask. Every time the mask becomes full, the current substring qualifies - and so do all further extensions within the run.
s: Map a, e, i, o, u to bit positions 0-4.
For each start whose character is a vowel, scan right until a non-vowel or the end of the string.
OR the current character bit into the mask.
Increment the answer whenever the mask equals 31.
a.t: O(n^2) - each start scans forward through its vowel run
a.sp: O(1) - a bitmask and loop indices

a.n: Approach 2: Linear Sliding Window With atMost(k)
a.i: Let g(k) be the number of vowel-only substrings containing at most k distinct vowels. Substrings with all five vowels number exactly g(5) - g(4), and each g(k) follows from a standard two-pointer sweep that resets whenever a consonant appears.
s: Implement atMost(k): sweep the right end; on a consonant, clear counts and jump left past it.
Otherwise add the incoming character to frequency counts and shrink from the left while distinct exceeds k.
Add right - left + 1 (windows ending at right) after each step.
a.t: O(n) - each index enters and leaves the window a constant number of times across two sweeps

w: For this constraint set the bitmask double loop is the simplest thing that can possibly work and is easy to defend in an interview; bring up atMost(k) when asked to scale. Pitfalls: letting a window shrink past a consonant instead of resetting, and accidentally counting substrings with only four distinct vowels. Natural follow-up: count substrings with exactly k distinct vowels for arbitrary k using the same subtraction.
